read: full: all 29 pages (abstract, introduction, methods, large-scale and small-scale supervision, OOD generalization, discussion, related work, appendices A-I)
venue_now: arXiv 2305.20050v1, 31 May 2023 (p.1 footer); this text shows no venue. papers.json records ICLR 2024 (poster); the May reference list prints 'ArXiv preprint, abs/2305.20050'.
what_it_is: A comparison of outcome supervision (feedback on the final result) and process supervision (feedback on each intermediate step) for training reward models that pick among GPT-4-generated solutions to MATH problems (p.1-3). Human labellers marked each step of model-generated solutions positive, negative or neutral; the released PRM800K holds about 800K step labels on 75K solutions to 12K problems after filtering (p.4), 1,085,590 labels on 101,599 solutions before it (p.17). Reward models are evaluated by best-of-N selection graded on the final answer, on 500 held-out MATH test problems (p.3, p.5): the process-supervised reward model (PRM) solves 78.2% against 72.4% for the outcome-supervised one (ORM) and 69.6% for majority voting at best-of-1860 (p.7). Small-scale runs use the large PRM as a synthetic labeller, and active learning makes process supervision about 2.6 times more data-efficient (p.2, p.9).
domain: competition mathematics (MATH), with an out-of-distribution check on recent AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics and AMC10/12 problems (p.10)
size: PRM800K: about 800K step labels, 75K solutions, 12K problems after filtering (p.4); 1,085,590 labels on 101,599 solutions unfiltered (p.17). Test: 500 MATH test problems (p.5, p.18); OOD set: '224 STEM questions' in the text but 234 in Table 1 (p.10). Generator and reward models fine-tuned from GPT-4, plus small-scale models pretrained with roughly 200 times less compute (p.3).
source_of_items: competitions: MATH problems (4.5K MATH test problems were moved into training, p.5); solutions sampled from a GPT-4-based generator and labelled step by step by human data-labellers (p.4)
instances: static (fixed MATH problems; the labelled solutions are model samples)
has_gold_traces: partial: human step-level correctness labels (positive, negative, neutral) on model-generated solutions, in phase 2 only up to the first negative step (p.4, p.6, p.19). Labellers saw the ground-truth final answer but deliberately no reference solution, 'to avoid biasing them towards one particular path to the solution' (p.19). No gold reasoning trace is used.
evaluation: best-of-N: the reward model selects one of N sampled solutions, which is graded automatically on its final answer (p.3 sec. 2.1, p.7). The PRM's step-level accuracy against held-out human step labels is not reported.
human_validation: Labeller screening only: before phase 2 every labeller did 30 quality-control questions and was admitted only at 75% or more agreement with the researchers' gold labels; 10-20 quality-control problems per generation were served afterwards to remove labellers whose quality slipped (p.17-18). No inter-annotator agreement is reported.
contamination_measures: string-matching and n-gram decontamination of the MathMix pretraining mix against the MATH test set, with no strong guarantee claimed (p.11, p.16); evaluation restricted to 500 held-out MATH problems (p.5); recency check on AP and AMC exams released after the pretraining data was compiled (p.10)

engtrace_use.sentence: Inspired by recent advances in process supervision (Lightman et al., 2023) and cascaded model verification (Chen et al., 2023), we introduce a two-stage evaluation framework that validates intermediate reasoning steps in addition to final-answer accuracy through a tiered verification protocol. (sec. 4, May L390-395)
engtrace_use.explanation: The clause credits the paper only with being an advance in process supervision, which it is: it defines process supervision as feedback on each intermediate reasoning step and shows it trains more reliable reward models than outcome supervision (p.1-2, p.7). Caveats for the rewrite: (1) in the paper 'process supervision' is the supervision given to a reward model in training (p.3 sec. 2.1), and the reward model is judged by best-of-N selection graded on the final answer (p.3), not by step-level accuracy; EngTrace evaluates traces, so the revised text should keep 'process supervision' for the training signal and say 'step-level evaluation' or 'step verification' for its own method. (2) The two-stage tiered protocol the sentence introduces no longer exists (the evaluator is now deterministic checks plus a residual judge, state brief sec. 2), so the sentence must be rewritten whatever the verdict, and 'recent' no longer fits a 2023 paper. (3) The reference entry (May L1061-1071) prints 30 names, 23 of them not authors (e.g. Lukas Mesnard, Tyna Wang; Wojciech Zaremba is only thanked, p.13), and omits Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee and Karl Cobbe; p.1 lists 10 authors. The citation still points at the right paper (title and arXiv id are correct).

suggested_wording: Process supervision, feedback on each intermediate step rather than on the final answer, trains more reliable reward models for competition mathematics than outcome supervision, but its roughly 800K step labels had to come from human annotators because there is 'no simple way to automate process supervision' (Lightman et al., 2023); EngTrace's templates compute the intermediate values, so numeric milestones can be checked deterministically.
facts_to_cite: Process supervision gives feedback on each intermediate reasoning step; outcome supervision gives feedback only on the final result (p.1, p.2).
At best-of-1860 on a 500-problem MATH test subset, the process-supervised reward model solves 78.2%, the outcome-supervised one 72.4% and majority voting 69.6% (p.5, p.7).

PRM800K, released with the paper, holds about 800K human step-level labels on 75K model-generated solutions to 12K MATH problems after filtering (p.4), 1,085,590 labels on 101,599 solutions before filtering (p.17).
Step labels came from human data-labellers because 'there is no simple way to automate process supervision' (p.3).

Grading by final answer misgrades solutions that reach the correct answer with incorrect reasoning (p.5, p.8); the paper notes, citing prior work, that outcome-supervised models regularly use incorrect reasoning to reach correct answers (p.2).
Labellers were given the final answer but not a reference solution, to avoid biasing them towards one solution path (p.19).
Reward models are evaluated by best-of-N selection graded on the final answer (p.3).
Active learning that surfaces convincing wrong-answer solutions made process supervision about 2.6 times more data-efficient (p.2, p.9).
The authors leave open how far the results generalise beyond mathematics (p.11) and expect easy-to-check final answers not to remain available in more complex domains (p.6).
Out of distribution, on recent AP and AMC problems, the PRM reaches 72.9% aggregate against the ORM's 63.8% and majority voting's 61.3% at best-of-100 (Table 1, p.10).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: judging reasoning step by step, and the argument that final-answer grading misses incorrect reasoning inside correct answers (p.2, p.5), which EngTrace measures directly (93 of 228 correct-answer traces in X1 contain an incorrect step, state brief sec. 3). Lacks: generated instances (fixed MATH problems), gold reasoning traces (labellers saw only the final answer, p.19), engineering content (mathematics only; generalisation left open, p.11), any deterministic check of steps (its step labels are human judgements), and a step-level evaluation of its own reward model (judged through final-answer best-of-N, p.3). It is a training-method and dataset paper, not a benchmark. The link to EngTrace is concrete: EngTrace's PRM measurements include VersaPRM, a LoRA on Llama-PRM800K, i.e. a model trained on this paper's data (state brief sec. 3 and 6).
notes: Batch V question: in the planned paragraph on process supervision and judge validity this is the anchor citation for (a) the process-versus-outcome distinction, (b) PRM800K as the human-labelled step data that PRMs are trained on, including the VersaPRM base EngTrace measured (step AUROC 0.629, recall 0.064, state brief sec. 3), and (c) the cost argument that step labels need humans because steps cannot be checked automatically (p.3). EngTrace's template-computed milestones and digit rule close that gap for numeric steps only: no deterministic check catches any of the 60 conceptual plants (state brief sec. 3), so the revised text must not say EngTrace automates process supervision. Do not cite this paper for evaluating models' reasoning or for step-level metrics; it reports none. Its choice to withhold reference solutions to avoid path bias (p.19) is worth acknowledging where EngTrace explains how it handles alternative valid paths (order-free milestones, residual judge). Internal inconsistency: the OOD set is '224 STEM questions' in the text but Table 1 sums to 234 (45+60+45+84) (p.10); quote neither. The abstract rounds the headline to 78% (p.1); the body gives 78.2% (p.2, p.7). Reference list: correct the author list to the 10 on p.1; the venue (ICLR 2024 per papers.json) is not visible in this arXiv v1 text.
